abstracts.abstract: Traditional security protocol verification relies heavily on computational complexity assumptions that fail to capture emerging threats in distributed systems. This paper introduces the Observable State Transition Framework (OSTF), a fundamentally novel approach to security verification that transcends conventional symbolic and computational models. Unlike existing methodologies that analyze protocols in isolation, OSTF models security properties as dynamic observable behaviors across interconnected system components. We formalize the notion of security as emergent properties arising from protocol composition, establishing new theoretical foundations based on game-theoretic interactions among protocol participants. Our framework enables verification of properties previously considered undecidable, including temporal privacy guarantees and adaptive trust evolution. The mathematical formalization demonstrates that OSTF can verify infinite-state protocols through finite observable abstractions. We prove the soundness and completeness of our verification procedure and establish complexity bounds that show significant advantages over model checking approaches. The theoretical contribution includes novel proof techniques that decompose complex security proofs into observable invariants, enabling mechanical verification of sophisticated protocols. This work represents a paradigm shift from trace-based verification toward behavior-based security assessment, opening new research directions in formal methods for complex distributed architectures.

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) models face significant limitations when handling temporal constraints in dynamic organizational environments. Existing temporal extensions of RBAC introduce excessive complexity, making administration impractical for large-scale systems. This paper presents the Temporal Hierarchical Role Model (THRM), which significantly extends the expressive power of RBAC while maintaining administrative tractability. We introduce novel temporal role concepts including activation windows, delegation constraints, and permission inheritance rules that operate across time dimensions. The formal semantics of THRM are defined using first-order temporal logic, enabling precise specification of when roles can be activated, delegated, or inherited. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that THRM subsumes existing temporal RBAC models while reducing administrative operations by an order of magnitude through hierarchical temporal abstractions. We prove that critical security properties including separation of duty and least privilege are preserved across temporal role activations. The paper establishes complexity results showing that THRM administration remains polynomial-time decidable, addressing the computational barriers that limited previous temporal extensions. Comparative analysis with state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates THRM's superior expressiveness-to-complexity ratio, providing organizations with a practical foundation for implementing fine-grained temporal access control policies in enterprise systems.

Privacy-preserving computation in multi-party scenarios remains challenging due to the fundamental tension between data utility and confidentiality. This paper presents PrivacyChain, a novel system architecture that integrates confidential computing enclaves with permissioned blockchain technology to enable verifiably private data sharing across organizational boundaries. Unlike prior approaches that rely on cryptographic obfuscation alone, PrivacyChain establishes a hardware-backed trust foundation combined with distributed ledger verification. The system architecture comprises three innovative components: an enclave-based computation layer that executes smart contracts within Intel SGX protected memory, a privacy-preserving cross-chain communication protocol enabling secure data exchange without revealing transaction contents, and a reputation-based access control mechanism that dynamically adjusts data access permissions based on participant behavior history. We implement a fully functional prototype demonstrating privacy-preserving collaborative machine learning across healthcare data sources without exposing individual patient records. Evaluation results show that PrivacyChain achieves transaction throughput of 3,400 operations per second with average latency of 280 milliseconds, representing substantial improvements over existing privacy-preserving blockchain systems. The system provides formal privacy guarantees verifiable through the blockchain, establishing a new paradigm for building trustworthy distributed applications that protect sensitive information while maintaining the auditability benefits of distributed ledger technology.

Network intrusion detection systems increasingly struggle against sophisticated attacks that evade signature-based detection while avoiding behavioral thresholds used by anomaly detection methods. This paper presents DeepShield, an advanced intrusion detection system that significantly improves detection accuracy through a hierarchical deep learning architecture specifically designed for encrypted network traffic analysis. The system architecture employs a novel multi-scale temporal convolutional network that extracts both local packet patterns and global flow characteristics without requiring traffic decryption. DeepShield incorporates an attention-based mechanism that highlights network behaviors indicative of sophisticated threats, enabling security analysts to understand detection rationales through explainable outputs. We design a distributed deployment architecture that enables real-time analysis at enterprise scale with minimal latency overhead. The system includes a continuously updating detection model that adapts to emerging attack patterns through federated learning, allowing collaborative threat intelligence sharing without compromising individual network data. Evaluation against comprehensive datasets demonstrates that DeepShield achieves 99.2% detection accuracy with only 0.3% false positive rate, improving detection rates for advanced persistent threats by 47% compared to state-of-the-art methods. The system's inference latency of 2.3 milliseconds per flow enables deployment in high-speed network environments without performance degradation, providing organizations with significantly enhanced capability to detect and respond to sophisticated network attacks.
